title: Vitamin C Injections in Brooklyn: Published Prices and Fees
description: Compare Brooklyn vitamin C injections at $30 and $45, including a separate nurse consultation fee that affects first-visit cost. Updated October 2026.
main_html:
Brooklyn, New York · price comparison · checked October 28, 2026

Vitamin C injections in Brooklyn: two published prices under $100, and the consultation fee that changes the first-visit total.

Quick answer

W8MD publishes a vitamin C intramuscular (IM) injection starting at $30 in Sheepshead Bay. Allergy & Asthma Care of Brooklyn publishes a $45 vitamin C injection, but its separately listed one-time nurse consultation is $40 for non-allergy patients, making the listed first-visit components $85 before any other charges. Prices and appointment availability must be confirmed directly with each clinic.

This is an independent editorial comparison. Neither clinic is represented as a paying advertiser, a verified lead recipient, or an endorsed provider. A callback from this guide is not a booking with either clinic.

What this guide is best for

This guide is best for someone in Brooklyn who has already decided they want a vitamin C injection and wants to know what it actually costs on the day, including the fees that sit outside the advertised price. It compares the only two Brooklyn clinics we could find publishing a standalone vitamin C injection price, explains why the cheaper headline number is not automatically the cheaper visit, and gives you the questions that turn an advertised price into a confirmed total. It is not a directory of every Brooklyn clinic, not a ranking, not a booking service, and not medical advice about whether an injection is right for you.

How do you turn two advertised prices into comparable totals?

The two published prices on this page are not describing the same purchase, which is why subtracting one from the other tells you very little. One is a starting price subject to medical review; the other is a fixed injection price with a separately listed one-time consultation. To compare them properly, ask each clinic for the same five numbers:

  1. The price of the injection itself, for the dose and route you want.
  2. Every fee charged on a first visit that is not the injection — consultation, evaluation, intake, or supplies.
  3. Whether that first-visit fee repeats on later visits or is genuinely one-time.
  4. The price of a second and third injection, if you intend to return.
  5. What is charged if you are screened and then told an injection is not appropriate for you.

The fifth question is the one most people skip and the one most likely to produce an unexpected charge. A clinic that screens you, declines to inject, and bills the consultation has done nothing wrong — but you should know that before you go, not after.

Set against those five numbers, a single visit at the $30 starting price may or may not be cheaper than a single visit at $45 plus a $40 one-time consultation; a course of several injections almost certainly changes the answer again, because a one-time fee spreads across repeat visits while a per-injection price does not.

Which is closer to Bed-Stuy or 251 Tompkins Avenue?

The Plaza Street East location near Grand Army Plaza is geographically closer to Bedford-Stuyvesant than W8MD's Sheepshead Bay office. Exact travel time depends on your starting point and transit conditions; check a current route before booking. We have not verified another nearby Brooklyn clinic offering standalone vitamin C IM injections at a published price.

Five questions before you pay

  1. Is this a vitamin C intramuscular injection rather than an IV drip, IV push, or an add-on?
  2. What is the total first-visit price, including consultation, supplies, and administration?
  3. What dose and formulation will be used, and is it in stock on the appointment date?
  4. Who screens kidney history, medications, allergies, pregnancy status when relevant, and whether an injection is appropriate?
  5. Can I book directly, and what is the cancellation policy?

What should you check about your own history before booking?

Parenteral vitamin services are screened services, so the information you bring affects both your safety and whether the visit can go ahead at all. Before booking, be ready to describe any kidney disease or history of kidney stones; any known G6PD deficiency, which matters for certain formulations and doses; allergies, including to preservatives and additives; your current medications and supplements; pregnancy status where applicable; and the reason you want the injection. If you have had recent bloodwork relevant to deficiency or kidney function, have the results available rather than describing them from memory. If you are not sure whether something is relevant, say it anyway and let the clinician decide.

Injection and infusion safety

Medical history matters before any parenteral vitamin service. Ask about kidney disease, kidney stones, a history of G6PD deficiency when relevant to the planned formulation and dose, allergies, medication interactions, pregnancy where applicable, and the reason for treatment. Sterile technique, qualified administration, and a plan for reactions matter. Vitamin injections have risks and are not established general-purpose immune boosters.

Who should consider an evaluation instead?

Someone with persistent fatigue, suspected deficiency, recurrent illness, or a significant medical condition may need a clinician assessment and appropriate testing before deciding on an injection. Most people who can absorb and take oral vitamin C do not need injections simply to meet ordinary nutritional needs. Ask the clinician to explain why the proposed route makes sense for your situation.

Booking red flags

  • A price that excludes an undisclosed required consultation or setup charge.
  • Marketing that equates an IM shot with an IV drip or claims disease prevention or cure.
  • No screening, no licensed clinician identification, or no clear aftercare instructions.
  • A promise that a directory callback is a confirmed clinic appointment.

Which timing and payment details belong in the comparison?

Ask how far out the next appointment is, since a price you cannot use for three weeks is not comparable to one you can use on Friday. Ask whether the dose and formulation you were quoted is in stock on your appointment date, and what the clinic does if it is not. Ask when payment is taken relative to screening, which methods are accepted, and what the cancellation and no-show policy costs. Ask whether you can book directly rather than through a third party, and get the name of the clinician or nurse who will administer the injection. None of these changes the advertised price, and all of them change what the visit is worth.

Vitamin C injection vs. IV drip

An IM injection is administered into a muscle; an IV infusion goes into a vein. An inexpensive injection should not be presented as a vitamin C IV drip. The routes have different fees, procedures, and risks. Neither method is automatically preferable to oral vitamin C, and neither is a substitute for evaluation of persistent symptoms or nutritional deficiency.

How do you decide when a quote is still incomplete?

Treat a quote as incomplete when it names a price but not the route — an intramuscular injection and an intravenous drip are different procedures at different prices — or when it does not say whether a consultation or intake fee applies on the first visit. It is also incomplete when it will not state the dose and formulation, when it leaves the repeat-visit price unsaid, when nobody will name the administering clinician, or when the clinic will not say what is charged if screening rules you out. Any one of those is reason enough to make a second call before you pay.

Next steps

Review the two direct source links and call each clinic to request the exact total for the route and dose you want. Compare verified appointment availability and whether any screening fee is extra. If you have symptoms or a suspected deficiency, seek a medical assessment before purchasing a wellness shot.
